advances: Ordinary three-dimensional volume on an explicit frustum. The calculation gives the all-normal lower bound and exact active menu, which are not supplied by the same-body near-quantile upper-bound argument alone.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
The triangle has area $9/2$ and centroid zero. Its dilations have affine defining inequalities in $(x,t)$, so $K_\varepsilon$ is compact and convex, with $Y$ in its interior. Let $F_n(q)$ denote the fraction of $T$ where $n\cdot X\ge q$. The centered triangle case of accepted fact 6a7d56e450b3126f gives $F_n(q)+F_n(-q)\ge8/9$ for every real $q$. For the scaled vertex values $2,-R,R-2$, the top-vertex tail, for $R-2\le q\le2$ when $R<4$, is the similar-triangle area
$$
F_n(q)=\frac{(2-q)^2}{(R+2)(4-R)}.
$$
Below the middle vertex value $R-2$, subtract the bottom-vertex triangle with fraction $(q+R)^2/[(R+2)(2R-2)]$, for $-R\le q\le R-2$ and $R>1$. The density from the two quadratic pieces is bounded by their common peak $2/(R+2)\le2/3$; if a denominator vanishes at a tied vertex use the remaining branch and the same bound. In particular $F_n(0)=4/(9-s^2)$ for $R\le2$, while for $R\ge2$ it is $1-R^2/[(R+2)(2R-2)]\ge1/2$ (the difference from $1/2$ is $(R-2)/[(R+2)(2R-2)]$). Also when $s\le1/4$ and $|q|\le1/4$ both tails use the top formula and sum to $(8+2q^2)/(9-s^2)$.

In the product $T\times[-1,1]$ at $(0,0)$ the cap fraction is $P_0=(1/2)\int_0^1[F_n(\beta t)+F_n(-\beta t)]\,dt$ for $n\ne0$. Outside the stated local region it exceeds $\gamma$ by at least $\delta$. For $|\beta|\ge72$, since $|n\cdot X|\le4$, a whole interval of heights of length at least $1-4/|\beta|$ is captured, giving $P_0\ge17/36$. For $|\beta|\le72$ and $s\ge1/4$, $F_n(0)\ge\gamma+\Delta$ with $\Delta=64/143-4/9=4/1287$. The density bound gives paired sum at least $2F_n(0)-(4/3)|\beta|t$, hence at least $2\gamma+\Delta$ on $[0,\Delta/96]$. Using the paired bound elsewhere gives excess at least $\Delta^2/192=\delta$. For $s<1/4$ and $1/4\le|\beta|\le72$, the exact local paired formula supplies excess at least $2\beta^2t^2/9$ in the paired sum on $[0,1/(4|\beta|)]$. Its half-integral is $1/(1728|\beta|)\ge1/124416>\delta$. A pure vertical normal has $P_0=1/2$.

Set $r(t)=1+\varepsilon t$ and $I_2=\int_{-1}^1r(t)^2dt=2(1+\varepsilon^2/3)$. Normalized frustum volume is the law of $(r(t)X,t)$ with independent uniform $X$ on $T$ and height density $r(t)^2/I_2$. For the cap through $Y$, its margin is $n\cdot X+\beta t+\varepsilon(t\,n\cdot X-\beta/3)$. Under uniform height, the original margin $n\cdot X+\beta t$ has density at most $\min(2/3,1/(2|\beta|))$ by convolution (use $2/3$ for $\beta=0$). A changed sign lies within distance $\varepsilon(4+|\beta|/3)$ of zero. The probability of this band is at most $(17/3)\varepsilon$: the upper bound is $\varepsilon(4+|\beta|/3)\min(4/3,1/|\beta|)$, maximized at $|\beta|=3/4$. The height density relative to uniform differs from one by at most $[2\varepsilon+(2/3)\varepsilon^2]/(1+\varepsilon^2/3)\le(7/3)\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon\le1/2$. For pure vertical normals the uniform-height sign change costs only $\varepsilon/6$. Thus $|P_\varepsilon-P_0|\le8\varepsilon$ in every direction, proving the exterior gap.

For $s\le1/4$ and $|\beta|\le1/4$, the physical threshold $-\beta(t-t_*)$ has magnitude at most $7/24$ since $|t-t_*|\le7/6$; the closer negative vertex value has magnitude at least $3/8$ since $r(t)\ge1/2$ and $R-2\le-3/4$. The positive vertex is farther from zero. Every slice therefore uses the isolated top-vertex formula. The resulting fraction is
$$
\frac{\int_{-1}^1[2r(t)+\beta(t-t_*)]^2dt}{(9-s^2)I_2}
=\frac{4+\beta^2/3}{9-s^2},
$$
because $\int_{-1}^1r(t)(t-t_*)dt=0$ and $\int_{-1}^1(t-t_*)^2dt=I_2/3$. Equality with $\gamma$ requires $s=0$, $\beta=0$, which gives precisely the three oriented normals listed. A cap containing the interior mark with boundary not through it contains a positive-volume extra slab over the parallel through-mark cap, so it cannot be active.

To prove uniqueness, if $x\ne0$ at a mark $(x,t_0)$ one of the three canonical horizontal forms is strictly positive there, since they sum to zero and span the plane. Its cap through that mark is strictly smaller on each positive-area slice than its cap through the axis, whose fraction is $\gamma$. At $(0,t_0)$ with $t_0\ne t_*$ a sufficiently small vertical tilt of a canonical horizontal cap stays in the same slice regime and its numerator has nonzero linear coefficient in the tilt, proportional to $\int_{-1}^1r(t)(t-t_0)dt=2(t_*-t_0)$. Choose the opposite sign to reduce the cap below $\gamma$. This proves uniqueness.

statement:
Let $T=\operatorname{conv}\lbrace(2,-1),(-1,2),(-1,-1)\rbrace$ and $K_\varepsilon=\lbrace(x,t):|t|\le1,\ x\in(1+\varepsilon t)T\rbrace$, where $0<\varepsilon\le10^{-9}$. Put $t_*=\varepsilon/3$, $Y=(0,t_*)$, $\gamma=4/9$, and $\delta=1/19{,}876{,}428$. The unique ordinary deepest point is $Y$, with depth $\gamma$ for normalized volume. The only active closed halfspaces at $Y$ pass through it and have inward normals positive multiples of $(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(-1,-1,0)$.

For a normal $(n,\beta)$ with $n\ne0$, scale it positively so that the largest of the three $n$-values at the vertices is $2$. Order the others as $-R,R-2$ with $1\le R\le4$, and put $s=R-1$. If $s\le1/4$ and $|\beta|\le1/4$, the actual through-$Y$ cap fraction is $(4+\beta^2/3)/(9-s^2)$. Every other direction, including pure vertical normals, has through-$Y$ cap fraction at least $\gamma+\delta-8\varepsilon>\gamma$.
title: The exact deepest point and full active cap menu of a triangle frustum
